claims.text: A two-step thermal treatment consisting of low-temperature annealing followed by a high-temperature pulse governs formation of a uniform single-phase solid solution in noble-metal-based HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
The staged treatment decouples the kinetics of atomic mobility from crystallization.
Decoupling atomic mobility from crystallization reduces elemental segregation and morphological irregularities relative to a one-step rapid thermal cycle.
The starting material is a solid, single-source precursor in which more than five noble metals are mixed at the atomic scale.
Annealing at approximately 200 °C for approximately 10 minutes enables precursor atomic rearrangement.
Carefully calibrated annealing near 200 °C can avoid premature crystallite growth.
A brief pulse at 500–600 °C triggers crystallization after the low-temperature rearrangement stage.
Low-temperature annealing produces prior microstructural ordering that promotes uniform nucleation during the high-temperature pulse.
Limited thermal energy at the low-temperature stage permits controlled atomic rearrangement without significant diffusion-driven phase separation.
Low-temperature preordering reduces kinetic traps.
The high-temperature pulse overcomes the remaining activation barriers.
The high-temperature stage drives uniform crystallization into a single-phase structure.
Rapid cooling locks in the single-phase structure formed during the high-temperature pulse.
Relative to one-step rapid heating and cooling, the two-step process produces a more uniform single-phase crystal structure.
Relative to the one-step baseline, the two-step process minimizes elemental segregation, controls grain size, and reduces morphological irregularities.
Single-step thermal decomposition with rapid heating and cooling often causes phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled particle morphology.
The hypothesis applies to rapidly thermally cycled noble-metal-based HEA nanoparticle systems containing more than five elements.
An excessively long annealing dwell can cause excessive grain growth.
Insufficient annealing time fails to produce the precursor ordering needed for uniform nucleation.
The optimal temperatures and dwell times are undetermined and may vary with synthesis conditions.
